x: The English East India Company was established in 1600 under a royal charter. 1757 is Plassey, 1764 is Buxar and 1773 is the Regulating Act.
t: Recall the founding year of the Company.

x: The East India Company was an English joint-stock trading company, owned by merchant shareholders, not a royal department, a French body or a revenue council.
t: Recall the nature of the Company.

x: Queen Elizabeth I granted the royal charter on 31 December 1600. George III and Victoria reigned much later, and William Pitt was a Prime Minister, not a monarch.
t: Match the charter year with the reigning monarch.

x: The Company's early objective was eastern trade, especially in spices and textiles. Territorial rule over Bengal came only after 1757.
t: Separate the Company's early trading aim from its later political role.

x: Bengal became the Company's first major territorial base after Plassey (1757) and the grant of Diwani (1765). Madras and Bombay were trading settlements, not large territories.
t: Link Plassey and Diwani to the first territorial base.

x: Plassey was fought in 1757, Buxar in 1764, Diwani rights came in 1765 and the Regulating Act in 1773, giving A, B, C, D.
t: Arrange the events by year.

x: Both are true: the Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company's commercial functions, and the Government of India Act of 1858 ended Company rule and transferred power to the Crown.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All four are connected: spices and textiles were the Company's early trade objective, while tea and the China trade were the monopolies kept by the Charter Act of 1813.
t: Recall the exceptions kept by the 1813 Charter Act.

x: The Regulating Act was 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, the Charter Act 1813 and the Government of India Act 1858, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the year of each Act.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Treaty of Allahabad was concluded in 1765, not 1782. It followed Buxar and involved Clive, Shah Alam II and Shuja-ud-Daula; 1782 is the Treaty of Salbai.
t: Check the year in each statement.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Treaty of Mangalore (1784) ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War, but its date only tells when, not why it ended the war.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The Treaty of Madras was 1769, Allahabad 1765, Salbai 1782 and Bassein 1802, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the year of each treaty.

x: Both are true: the Treaty of Bassein (1802) was signed by Peshwa Baji Rao II with the British, and under it he accepted the Subsidiary Alliance.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: I, II and III are correct: Amritsar (1809) was between Ranjit Singh and the British, Sugauli (1815) between the British and Nepal, and Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War.
t: Check the year and parties of each treaty.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Treaty of Amritsar was concluded in 1809 between Ranjit Singh and the British.
II. The Treaty of Sugauli was concluded in 1815 between the British and Nepal.
III. The Treaty of Yandabo ended the First Anglo-Burmese War.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Allahabad was 1765, Madras 1769, Salbai 1782 and Srirangapatna 1792, giving B, A, C, D.
t: Arrange the treaties by year.

x: All five ended wars: Madras, Mangalore and Srirangapatna ended the first three Anglo-Mysore Wars, Sugauli the Anglo-Nepal War and Yandabo the First Anglo-Burmese War.
t: Check which war each treaty ended.
s: How many of the following treaties are specifically associated with ending a war? 1. Treaty of Madras 2. Treaty of Mangalore 3. Treaty of Srirangapatna 4. Treaty of Sugauli 5. Treaty of Yandabo

x: Srirangapatna was between Tipu Sultan and Cornwallis, Bassein between Peshwa Baji Rao II and the British, Amritsar between Ranjit Singh and the British, and Lahore ended the First Anglo-Sikh War, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the parties or war linked to each treaty.

x: The Treaty of Lahore was signed in 1846 after the First Anglo-Sikh War. 1809 is Amritsar, 1815 Sugauli and 1826 Yandabo.
t: Recall the year of the treaty.

x: Option D is incorrect: the Treaty of Yandabo (1826) was between the British and Burma and ended the First Anglo-Burmese War. The British–Nepal treaty was Sugauli (1815).
t: Discriminate Yandabo from Sugauli.

x: Both are true: the Treaty of Lahore (1846) followed the First Anglo-Sikh War and extended British control in Punjab, and the Treaty of Sugauli (1815) ended the Anglo-Nepal War.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Madras ended the First Anglo-Mysore War, Mangalore ended the Second, Salbai made British–Maratha peace and Amritsar fixed the Sutlej boundary, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the outcome of each treaty.

x: Bassein was 1802, Amritsar 1809, Sugauli 1815 and Yandabo 1826, giving A, B, C, D.
t: Arrange the treaties by year.

x: Three were Anglo-Mysore treaties: Madras (1769), Mangalore (1784) and Srirangapatna (1792). Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War.
t: Discriminate Mysore treaties from Maratha treaties.

x: The Treaty of Srirangapatna (1792) between Tipu Sultan and Cornwallis ended the Third Anglo-Mysore War, and Tipu lost half his territory.
t: Link the year 1792 to the Third Anglo-Mysore War.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Treaty of Salbai was concluded in 1782, not 1802. It ended the First Anglo-Maratha War and brought British–Maratha peace; 1802 is the Treaty of Bassein.
t: Discriminate Salbai from Bassein.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Indian High Courts Act of 1861 empowered the Crown to set up High Courts and abolished the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats, so the High Courts replaced both under that Act.
t: Ask whether the Reason names the law that brought about the Assertion.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the High Courts were set up by Letters Patent, which were instruments issued under the authority of the Crown.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: I, II and III are correct: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts were the first set, set up in 1862. IV is false because the Allahabad High Court came later, in 1866.
t: Recall which High Courts were set up in 1862.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Calcutta High Court belonged to the first set of High Courts.
II. Bombay High Court belonged to the first set of High Courts.
III. Madras High Court belonged to the first set of High Courts.
IV. Allahabad High Court belonged to the first set of High Courts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: I, II and III are correct: Canning served from 1856 to 1862, as the last Governor-General under the Company and the first Viceroy under the Crown. IV is false because his term ended before the Allahabad High Court came in 1866.
t: Compare Canning's tenure with the 1866 date.
s:
Consider the following statements about Lord Canning:
I. His tenure mentioned in this context was 1856–1862.
II. He was the last Governor-General under the Company.
III. He was the first Viceroy under the Crown.
IV. He was associated with the Allahabad High Court established in 1866.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Canning's tenure began in 1856, the Indian High Courts Act came in 1861, the first High Courts were set up in 1862 and Allahabad High Court in 1866, giving D, B, C, A.
t: Arrange the events by year.

x: The Indian High Courts Act came in 1861, Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts were set up in 1862, and Allahabad followed in 1866. The other options mix up these years.
t: Arrange the Act and the courts by year.

x: Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General when the first railway opened in 1853, and his Railway Minute of 1853 planned the network. Canning, Cornwallis and Wellesley are not linked with it.
t: Link the 1853 railway to the Governor-General of the time.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Dalhousie's Railway Minute was issued in 1853 as a policy plan, and the first train ran on 16 April 1853; the opening is not the reason for the Minute.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The first railway ran from Bombay to Thane, the first in Eastern India from Howrah to Hooghly, the first in North India from Delhi to Agra, and it started at Bori Bunder, Bombay, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the route of each first railway line.

x: The first train ran on 16 April 1853, covered 34 km, carried passengers in a 14-coach train and was pulled by 3 steam locomotives, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the basic facts of the first train.

x: Faster movement means quicker movement, communication means exchange of information, administration means governance, and troop movement means movement of soldiers, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Match each reason with its meaning.

x: I, II and III are correct: faster movement, communication and troop movement were official reasons. IV is false because the colonial aim was to bring British goods into Indian markets, not to expand markets for Indian goods.
t: Separate official reasons from the colonial economic aim.

x: The first train ran from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane, so Thane was its destination. Bori Bunder was the starting point.
t: Discriminate the starting point from the destination.

x: The colonial economic aim was to carry raw materials to the ports for export and to carry British goods into Indian markets. The other options reverse or confuse this flow.
t: Trace the direction of goods under colonial trade.
